title: Day Dial
context: Grade 4, and the first place in the chapter where one clock time can mean two times of day. An adult sees a.m. and p.m. written after times, which is quickly learnt as a pair of labels. What is actually being settled is what they label: the half of the day before noon and the half after it. That decides the answer when a count of hours passes 12 noon or 12 midnight, where the label changes. A child who carries the old label writes a time twelve hours out. The printed exercise counts hours across noon both ways and forward from just after midnight.

writeup.why: Tell the two halves of a day apart, write a.m. or p.m. after a time, and count hours forward or back across noon and midnight.
writeup.look: A strip from one midnight to the next with a sun on the noon post, a clock whose hour hand turns with a marker, and a tray of day cards.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Day Dial' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the laps, cards or hops done against what this phase holds, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as the hour hand finishes a lap, a card settles or the hopper lands, and the second fixed at what this phase holds. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The clock stands at the top left of the working area, a face 220 across centred at 196,330, with its twelve numbers, sixty marks, a deep blue minute hand and a vermilion hour hand geared to the marker. The lap counter sits beside it, 200 by 56 at 340,236, reading first lap or second lap, and the day counter under it, 200 by 56 at 340,306. The tray of day cards stands at the top right, 560 by 150 at 580,226, each card 130 by 64 with a small picture of the activity and its time in ink and no label. The day strip runs across the lower half, 1056 by 100 at 80,540, twenty-four hour blocks of 44 each from the left-hand midnight post to the right-hand one: the twelve blocks before the noon post are sky blue and labelled a.m. under them, and the twelve after it are amber and labelled p.m. Each midnight post carries a moon and the noon post, at 608, carries a sun, and all three posts are near-black and stand taller than the strip. The marker is a near-black pin with a tag above it that carries its time with a.m. or p.m., and on a post the tag reads 12 noon or 12 midnight. The hopper works in the band over the strip, 1056 by 70 at 80,450, and draws each hop of one whole hour as a green arc from landing to landing, with the time written at each landing; a hop that crosses a post lights that post as it passes. Past the right-hand midnight post the strip slides left, the next day's strip slides in, and the day counter goes up by one; hopping back past the left-hand post brings in the day before. A pale pin can stand on the strip beside the marker to show where a child's answer would be. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve keys three across, the ten digits, a colon and a clear key, with two keys over it reading a.m. and p.m., and the answer slot holds a time with a label box after it that must be filled. On the first phase the slot takes a number alone; on the second the child drops each card and then fills its label. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own and are the pictures' colours too. The hour hand, every hour tile and hour cell, the hours column, and the hours of a time the stage splits into hours and minutes are vermilion. The minute hand, every minute tile and minute cell, the minutes column and the minutes of a split time are deep blue. The second hand, every second cell and the seconds column are reddish purple. The a.m. half of the day, from midnight to noon, is sky blue on every strip, timeline and track, and the p.m. half, from noon to midnight, is amber, so the label changes where the colour does. Time counted between a start and an end, every hop and total on a track, and the days counted between two dates are green. An hour or a minute carried or broken, with the digits it strikes and rewrites, is wine. A calendar day, week or year picked out or ticked, a month on its bar and a day tile are olive. The days left over beyond whole weeks, and the twenty-ninth of February in a leap year, are yellow outlined in near-black. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome: every clock rim, minute mark, clock number, hub, rule, tick, post, bracket, guide line and panel edge is near-black. Every reading survives with the colour taken away, because an hour hand is told from a minute hand by its length, a column by its heading, a half of the day by its label, and a counted day from one left out by being filled rather than outlined, before any of them is told by a colour. A figure that goes down by one is struck through once with the new figure written above it, and never rubbed out. The label on the marker's tag changes only when the marker crosses the noon post or a midnight post, and on the posts themselves the tag reads 12 noon or 12 midnight. The clock above shows the same face at a time and at the time twelve hours on, so the strip, not the clock, says which half of the day it is.
writeup.finish: The card shows the day strip with every hop the child made drawn over it, the noon and midnight posts they crossed lit, and the last time written with its label.

phases.win: the lap counter reaches two, and two places light on the strip where the clock shows the same time, one in each half
phases.does: slides the marker along the whole strip, counts the laps of the hour hand, then finds the two places on the strip where the clock shows the same time
phases.goal: a day has twenty-four hours and a clock shows twelve, so the hour hand goes round twice a day
phases.says: Slide from one midnight to the next. How many times does the hour hand go round?
phases.check: Away from the screen: the classroom clock shows three o'clock. Name something that could be happening at each of the two times it could be.
phases.feels: the whole strip is two laps of the same face, one in each half of the day
phases.hands: Lay a paper strip along the board marked midnight, noon and midnight again, with a moon at each end and a sun in the middle. Walk a card clock along it with the class, turning its hour hand one number for each hour, and count the laps aloud. Stop at seven in the morning and at seven in the evening, and hold the clock up both times.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: how many hours are there in one day? Second rung, the phase's: how many hours does one lap of the hour hand take? Third rung: the strip is cut to its morning half, from midnight to noon, and the child counts the laps on it before the whole day comes back. The pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: the face has every hour on it once, and one lap of the face looks like the whole day.
wrong.move: says the hour hand goes round once a day, so a clock showing seven can mean only one time.
wrong.screen: the marker slides from the left-hand midnight post, and at the noon post the lap counter reads one lap done with half the strip still ahead. The marker goes on to the right-hand post and the counter reaches two. The hour hand is then set at seven, and two places light on the strip, one in each half. The child's answer stays in the slot, nothing marked.

wrong.why: twenty-four is the number that belongs to a day, and a lap for each hour sounds like counting the hours.
wrong.move: says the hour hand goes round twenty-four times a day, once for each hour.
wrong.screen: the marker crosses one hour block and the hour hand moves on by one number, a twelfth of a lap and not a whole one. The marker is run on block by block, and the lap counter reaches its first lap only when the hand has passed all twelve numbers. The child's twenty-four stays in the slot beside the counter.

phases.screen: the clock above the day strip, with the marker on the left-hand midnight post and the lap counter at nought
phases.soWhat: The hour hand goes round twice a day, so a clock showing seven can mean seven in the morning or seven in the evening.

phases.win: every card settles in its half, and a.m. or p.m. is written after its time
phases.does: drops each card into the half of the day where it happens, then writes a.m. or p.m. after its time
phases.goal: times after midnight and before noon are a.m., and times after noon and before midnight are p.m.
phases.says: Does this happen before noon or after noon? Put it in that half.
phases.check: Write a.m. or p.m. for a school assembly at 9:10 and for an evening walk at 6:25.
phases.feels: the half of the day decides the label, and the number on the clock does not
phases.hands: Give each child a strip and six blank cards. Each writes a time and a thing done at it, such as brushing teeth or dinner, with no a.m. or p.m., and places the cards on the strip. Then they write the labels, reading the half each card sits in and not the size of its number.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: does this happen before noon or after noon? Second rung, the phase's: which half of the strip is that? Third rung: the tray is cut to two cards, one plainly in the morning and one plainly at night, before the rest come back. The a.m. and p.m. keys stay open.

wrong.why: the morning half begins with the small numbers after midnight, so a small number feels early.
wrong.move: writes 1:15 a.m. for lunch, because one is a small number and small numbers seem to come in the morning.
wrong.screen: the card settles where the child put it, an hour and a quarter after the left-hand midnight post, near the moon in the sky blue half. The same time after the noon post lights beside it in the amber half, and the card's word, lunch, is read aloud. The child's label stays on the card, nothing marked.

wrong.why: on the face the big numbers come last, so a big number feels like the end of the day.
wrong.move: writes 11:40 p.m. for a snack in the late morning, because eleven is a big number and big numbers seem to come late.
wrong.screen: the card settles where the child put it, twenty minutes before the right-hand midnight post, near the moon in the amber half. The same time twenty minutes before the noon post lights beside it in the sky blue half, under the sun, and the card's words are read aloud. The child's label stays on the card.

phases.screen: the day strip with its a.m. and p.m. halves, and a tray of day cards whose times carry no label
phases.soWhat: Times from midnight to noon are a.m., and times from noon to midnight are p.m.

phases.win: the label changes from a.m. to p.m. on the hop that crosses the noon post, and the end time is written
phases.does: hops the marker forward one hour at a time, reading the label at each landing, then hops back from an afternoon time
phases.goal: a count of hours that passes 12 noon changes a.m. to p.m., and a count back past noon changes p.m. to a.m.
phases.says: Hop one hour at a time. What happens to the label when you pass noon?
phases.check: What time is five hours after 9:40 a.m.? Say which hop crossed noon.
phases.feels: the label holds steady hop after hop in the morning, and turns over on the hop that crosses the sun
phases.hands: Mark a paper strip of the day in hours and stand a counter at 9 a.m. Have a child move it one hour at a time for five hours while the class says each time with its label. Stop at the noon post and ask what the next hop's label will be before anyone moves.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: where does the count start, and which way does it go? Second rung, the phase's: which hop crosses the noon post? Third rung: the count is cut to one hop that crosses noon, from an hour before it, before the longer count comes back. The pad and the label keys stay open.

wrong.why: the start had a.m. on it, and nothing in adding hours seems to touch the label.
wrong.move: keeps the a.m. label after the count passes noon, and writes 2:25 a.m. for six hours after 8:25 a.m.
wrong.screen: the hopper runs the six hops again one at a time, and the tag reads each landing aloud: 9:25 a.m., 10:25 a.m. and 11:25 a.m., then the fourth hop arcs over the noon post, which lights, and lands on 12:25 p.m. in the amber half. Two more hops land on 1:25 p.m. and 2:25 p.m. A pale pin shows the child's 2:25 a.m. near the moon in the sky blue half, and the child's answer stays in the slot.

wrong.why: one o'clock is where the numbers start again, so it feels like the place where the afternoon begins.
wrong.move: writes 12:25 a.m. for the landing one hour after 11:25 a.m., waiting for one o'clock before changing the label.
wrong.screen: the hop from 11:25 a.m. arcs over the noon post, which lights, and lands twenty-five minutes into the amber half, where the tag reads 12:25 p.m. A pale pin shows the child's 12:25 a.m. twenty-five minutes after the left-hand midnight post, at night, and the child's answer stays in the slot.

wrong.why: the start was p.m., and counting back feels like staying in the same afternoon.
wrong.move: keeps p.m. when counting four hours back from 2:35 p.m., and writes 10:35 p.m.
wrong.screen: the hopper turns and hops back one hour at a time, to 1:35 p.m. and 12:35 p.m., then over the noon post, which lights, to 11:35 a.m. in the sky blue half, and one more to 10:35 a.m. A pale pin shows the child's 10:35 p.m. late in the amber half, and the child's answer stays in the slot.

phases.screen: the marker at a morning time, the hopper set to a number of hours, and the noon post lit
phases.soWhat: A count of hours that passes 12 noon changes a.m. to p.m., and a count back past noon changes p.m. to a.m.

phases.win: the next day's strip slides in, the day counter goes up by one, and the label reads twelve and some minutes a.m.
phases.does: hops the marker past midnight into the next day, reads the new label, then hops back across midnight
phases.goal: the a.m. hours start at midnight, so twelve and a few minutes a.m. is just after midnight, at the start of a new day
phases.says: Hop past midnight. Is the new time just after noon, or just after midnight?
phases.check: What time is three hours after 10:20 p.m.? Say which day it falls on.
phases.feels: one hop over the midnight post turns the night into a new day and the label back to a.m.
phases.hands: Stand a counter on a paper strip at 11 p.m. and move it one hour on, past the midnight post onto a second strip laid beside the first. Ask what the time is and which day it is now. Then move it back an hour and ask again.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which post does the count cross? Second rung, the phase's: what label do the times just after midnight carry? Third rung: the count is cut to one hop from an hour before midnight, before the longer count comes back. The pad and the label keys stay open.

wrong.why: the start was p.m. and the count went forward, so it feels as if the evening is still going on.
wrong.move: keeps p.m. after passing midnight, and writes 1:35 p.m. for two hours after 11:35 p.m.
wrong.screen: the hopper runs the two hops again. The first arcs over the right-hand midnight post, which lights, the next day's strip slides in, the day counter goes up by one, and the tag reads 12:35 a.m. The second lands on 1:35 a.m. near the moon. A pale pin shows the child's 1:35 p.m. just past the sun on the new day's strip, and the child's answer stays in the slot.

wrong.why: twelve is the number on the noon post, and noon is the twelve o'clock a child is awake for.
wrong.move: reads 12:25 a.m. as twenty-five minutes after noon, because twelve o'clock sounds like the middle of the day.
wrong.screen: the marker is set at 12:25 a.m. and stands twenty-five minutes after the left-hand midnight post, near the moon, in the sky blue half. A pale pin stands twenty-five minutes after the noon post, where the tag would read 12:25 p.m., and both stay lit side by side with the child's answer in the slot.

wrong.why: the start was a.m., and going back an hour seems only to change the hour.
wrong.move: counts one hour back from 12:40 a.m. and writes 11:40 a.m., keeping the a.m. label.
wrong.screen: the hopper turns and hops back over the left-hand midnight post, which lights, the strip of the day before slides in from the left, and the tag reads 11:40 p.m. in the amber half, near the moon. A pale pin shows the child's 11:40 a.m. just before the sun, and the child's answer stays in the slot.

phases.screen: the marker near the right-hand end of the strip late at night, with the next day's strip waiting
phases.soWhat: A count that passes 12 midnight changes p.m. to a.m., and the time moves into the next day.

writeup.delight: The first phase, when the marker reaches the noon post. The hour hand has come back to the twelve with one lap done, and a thread is drawn from each morning hour block to the afternoon block the hour hand points the same way for, twelve threads arching over the sun. As the marker goes on into the afternoon each thread lights in turn when the marker reaches its far end, and the clock face above looks exactly as it did twelve hours before. It can be run as often as a finger likes, nothing is marked, and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase the marker stands on the left-hand midnight post under its moon, the hour hand of the clock above points at the twelve, and the lap counter reads nought. On the second the tray of day cards sits above the strip, each card an activity with a time and no label. On the third the marker stands at a morning time, the hopper is set to a number of hours, and the noon post is lit under its sun. On the fourth the marker stands late at night near the right-hand midnight post, with the edge of the next day's strip just showing past it. The running count at the top left holds the laps, the cards or the hops done against what this phase holds, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the marker, or the top card, or the hopper, or the right-hand midnight post, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks which half of the day it is. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: The whole strip and the next day's strip, the hopper both ways, the clock and the tray of day cards all open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on the two laps of the hour hand, writing a.m. or p.m., counting hours across noon, and times just after midnight.
voiceLines: A whole day on one strip, and a clock above it. Which half of the day are you in?
Slide from one midnight to the next. How many times does the hour hand go round?
Does this happen before noon or after noon? Put it in that half.
Hop one hour at a time. What happens to the label when you pass noon?
Hop past midnight. Is the new time just after noon, or just after midnight?
A new time. Find its half of the day before you hop.
Free play. The whole strip and the next day, with the hopper and the cards open.
Hop one hour at a time, and read the label at every landing.
Each card in its half, and each label changed on the hop that crossed a post.

observations.why: A day has twenty-four hours and the clock face shows twelve, so the hour hand needs two laps to get through one day.
observations.soWhat: The hour hand goes round twice a day, so a clock showing seven can mean seven in the morning or seven in the evening.
observations.observe: The lap counter reached two as the marker crossed from one midnight to the next, and two places lit on the strip where the clock looked the same.

observations.why: a.m. names the half from midnight to noon and p.m. the half from noon to midnight, whatever the number on the card.
observations.soWhat: Times from midnight to noon are a.m., and times from noon to midnight are p.m.
observations.observe: Each card settled in the half of the strip where its activity happens, and its label matched the colour under it.

observations.why: Every landing before the post is in the morning half, and the first landing after it is in the afternoon half.
observations.soWhat: A count of hours that passes 12 noon changes a.m. to p.m., and a count back past noon changes p.m. to a.m.
observations.observe: The label on the tag turned from a.m. to p.m. on the hop that crossed the noon post, and on none of the hops before it.

observations.why: The a.m. hours start at midnight, so the first hour of the new day is twelve and some minutes a.m.
observations.soWhat: A count that passes 12 midnight changes p.m. to a.m., and the time moves into the next day.
observations.observe: One hop past the right-hand midnight post brought in the next day's strip and a tag reading twelve and some minutes a.m.

source_tool.description: A day strip runs across the lower half of the working area from one midnight to the next, twenty-four hour blocks long. The half from midnight to noon is the a.m. half, with a moon at its left end, and the half from noon to midnight is the p.m. half, with a sun on the noon post between them. A clock face above the strip has its hour hand geared to a marker on the strip. Sliding the marker from one end to the other turns the hour hand round twice. A lap counter says which lap it is on. The marker carries its time with a.m. or p.m., and the label changes as the marker crosses the noon post or a midnight post; on the posts it reads 12 noon or 12 midnight. A hopper moves the marker a whole hour at a time, forward or back, drawing each hop as an arc over the strip. A hop that crosses noon or midnight is seen to cross it. Past the right-hand midnight post a second strip slides in for the next day, and a day counter goes up by one. A tray of day cards, each an activity with a time and no a.m. or p.m., waits to be dropped into the half of the day where it happens.
source_tool.art_direction: A day strip from moon to moon / Picture book

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a clock face with sixty marks, a strip of the day from one midnight to the next, a ladder of units with tiles, the page's own timeline, a column frame, a time track with flags and a hopper, and a wall of month cards.

Every clock is drawn exactly. The minute hand turns six degrees a minute and points exactly at a minute mark, and the hour hand turns thirty degrees an hour and half a degree a minute, so it sits exactly where the time puts it and never on a number except at the hour.

The minute hand is always the longer hand and the hour hand the shorter, and a second hand, where there is one, is the thinnest. A clock face always shows all twelve numbers and all sixty marks, with a longer mark at each number.
A time in figures is written with a colon and a.m. or p.m., as 4:40 p.m., and a 24-hour time as four digits and the word hours, as 1615 hours. Twelve o'clock is written 12 noon or 12 midnight.
Noon and midnight are drawn as posts wherever a strip, a timeline or a track crosses them, and a.m. changes to p.m., or back, only at a post.
A column of time carries at sixty. A carried or broken hour or minute is drawn as sixty cells in six rows of ten, never as ten or as a hundred.
A month card is the real month of the year shown, with its first day under the right weekday and the right number of days, as the calendar in use today lays out that year.
Every day count shows which of its ends it counts. A day that is counted is filled, and a day that is left out is outlined only, at full strength and never hidden.
Two answers being compared stand on the stage at the same time, one beside or above the other. An answer that has been replaced is never cleared away.
A hand, a column, a flag or a day is told apart by its shape, its label and its place first and by its colour second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a hand, a digit, a tile, a cell or a day the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. These are the chapter's own colours, taken from the pictures, so a tool and a picture of the same thing are the same colour. The hour hand, an hour tile, an hours column and the hours of a time split into hours and minutes are vermilion. The minute hand and every minute are deep blue, and the second hand and every second are reddish purple, following the page, whose hour hand is red and whose second hand is a thin pink. The a.m. half of the day, midnight to noon, is sky blue on every strip, timeline and track, and the p.m. half is amber, so the label changes where the colour does. Time counted between a start and an end, every hop and total on the duration track, and the days counted between two dates are green. An hour or a minute carried or broken, with the digits it strikes and rewrites, is wine. A calendar day, week or year picked out or ticked, a month on its bar and a day tile on the ladder are olive. The days left over beyond whole weeks, and the twenty-ninth of February in a leap year, are yellow outlined in near-black. Every clock rim, minute mark, number, hub, rule, tick, post, bracket and guide line is near-black chrome. All of that holds in greyscale, because an hour hand is told from a minute hand by its length, a column by its heading, a half of the day by its label, and a counted day from one left out by being filled rather than outlined.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Hop one hour at a time, and read the label at every landing.
voice.onNext: A new time. Find its half of the day before you hop.
voice.opening: A whole day on one strip, and a clock above it. Which half of the day are you in?
voice.onFinish: Each card in its half, and each label changed on the hop that crossed a post.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. The whole strip and the next day, with the hopper and the cards open.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

placement.where: After the class has laid its day out on a paper strip marked midnight, noon and midnight again, one card for each thing done. The tool turns the hour hand round twice as the marker crosses the strip. It changes the label at the exact hop that crosses noon or midnight, which a strip on a desk cannot do.

answer_key.rule: A day has twenty-four hours and a clock shows twelve, so the hour hand goes round twice a day. Times after midnight and before noon are a.m., short for ante meridiem, and times after noon and before midnight are p.m., short for post meridiem. Twelve o'clock in the middle of the day is 12 noon, and twelve o'clock at night is 12 midnight. A count of hours that passes 12 noon changes a.m. to p.m., and a count back past noon changes p.m. to a.m. A count that passes 12 midnight changes p.m. to a.m. and moves into the next day. A time such as 12:05 a.m. is five minutes after midnight, and 12:05 p.m. is five minutes after noon.
answer_key.wrong: The hopper runs the count again one hour at a time, and the label is read aloud at each landing. The hop that crosses noon or midnight is seen to be where the label changes. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: A day has twenty-four hours, but the clock face shows only twelve.
So the hour hand goes round twice in one day, once from midnight to noon and once from noon to midnight.
It points at the seven on both laps, so the clock alone cannot tell seven in the morning from seven in the evening.
items.answer: No. The hour hand goes round twice a day, so the clock shows seven o'clock once in the morning and once in the evening
items.question: A wall clock shows seven o'clock. Can you tell from the clock alone whether it is morning or evening?
items.checkpoint: The hour hand goes round twice a day, so a clock time such as seven o'clock comes once before noon and once after it.
items.misconception: Thinking the hour hand goes round once a day, so seven o'clock can mean only one time.

steps: Waking up happens in the morning, after midnight and before noon, so it is 6:10 a.m.
Lunch happens after noon, so it is 1:15 p.m.
The label depends on the half of the day, not on how big the number is.
items.question: A child wakes up at 6:10 and eats lunch at 1:15. Write a.m. or p.m. after each time.
items.checkpoint: Times after midnight and before noon are a.m., and times after noon and before midnight are p.m.
items.misconception: Writing 1:15 a.m. for lunch because one is a small number, as if small numbers meant morning.

steps: Hop one hour at a time: 9:25 a.m., 10:25 a.m. and 11:25 a.m. are the first three hops.
The fourth hop crosses 12 noon and lands on 12:25 p.m., so the label changes to p.m.
Two more hops land on 1:25 p.m. and then 2:25 p.m.
items.question: What time is six hours after 8:25 a.m.?
items.checkpoint: A count of hours that passes 12 noon changes a.m. to p.m.
items.misconception: Keeping the a.m. label after the count passes noon, and writing 2:25 a.m.

steps: One hour after 11:35 p.m. crosses 12 midnight and lands on 12:35 a.m., thirty-five minutes into a new day.
The label changes to a.m., because the a.m. hours start at midnight.
One more hour lands on 1:35 a.m.
items.question: What time is two hours after 11:35 p.m.?
items.checkpoint: A count that passes 12 midnight changes p.m. to a.m., and the time moves into the next day.
items.misconception: Keeping the p.m. label after passing midnight, and writing 1:35 p.m.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: How many hours are there in one day, and how many times does the hour hand go round in that time?
items.final_answer: Twenty-four hours, and the hour hand goes round twice

items.question: A shop opens at half past ten in the morning. Write the time with a.m. or p.m.
A family eats dinner at 8:35 in the evening. Write the time with a.m. or p.m.
What time is three hours after 10:50 a.m.?
items.final_answer: 1:50 p.m., because the count passes 12 noon

items.question: What time is four hours before 2:35 p.m.?
items.final_answer: 10:35 a.m., because counting back past 12 noon changes p.m. to a.m.

items.question: Is 12:25 a.m. just after noon or just after midnight?
items.final_answer: Just after midnight. It is twenty-five minutes into a new day

items.question: A child says three hours after 11:30 a.m. is 2:30 a.m. What is the right time, and what went wrong?
items.final_answer: 2:30 p.m. The count passed 12 noon, so the label should have changed from a.m. to p.m.

items.question: What time is one hour before 12:40 a.m.?
items.final_answer: 11:40 p.m. on the day before, because counting back past midnight changes a.m. to p.m.

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: runs from one midnight to the next, the a.m. half before the noon post and the p.m. half after it
slides along the strip carrying its time with a.m. or p.m.
turns its hour hand with the marker, twice round for the whole strip
says whether the hour hand is on its first or its second lap of the day
moves the marker one whole hour forward or back, drawing each hop over the strip
slides in past the right-hand midnight post and adds one to the day counter
each an activity with a time, dropped into the half of the day where it happens

teaching_notes: Lay a paper strip across the board marked midnight, noon and midnight again, and have the class place cards for the things they do in a day before the tool is opened. The page asks whether a clock showing nine means morning or night, and answers it with a.m. and p.m. in the next lines. Keep the answer tied to the halves of the strip and not to the size of the number, because one in the afternoon is p.m. and eleven in the morning is a.m. The twelve o'clock times need saying. 12 noon is the post between the halves, 12:05 p.m. is just after noon, and 12:05 a.m. is just after midnight, at the start of a new day. The exercise counts hours across noon both ways and forward from just after midnight, so hop an hour at a time and read the label at every landing. The hop that crosses a post is where the label changes.
generation_prompt: Build a day strip tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A strip twenty-four hour blocks long runs across the lower half of the working area from one midnight post to the next. The noon post in the middle is marked by a sun and each midnight post by a moon. The half before noon is labelled a.m. and the half after it p.m. A marker slides along the strip and carries its time with a.m. or p.m.; on the posts it reads 12 noon and 12 midnight. A clock face above the strip has its hour hand geared to the marker, so the whole strip turns it round exactly twice. A lap counter shows the first or second lap. A hopper moves the marker one whole hour forward or back and draws each hop as an arc over the strip. The label changes only on the hop that crosses the noon post or a midnight post. Past the right-hand midnight post a second strip slides in for the next day and a day counter rises by one. Hopping back past the left-hand post brings in the day before. A tray of day cards, each an activity with a time and no label, waits to be dropped into the half where it happens. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Slide the marker along the day. Watch the hour hand go round twice. Drop each card in its half. Hop one hour at a time. Read the label at every landing.
